comparison: Perfect agreement on retinotopic attentional modulation findings (C8, C30, C37-42, C107). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported. OpenEval notes the hierarchical strengthening is qualitative rather than formally tested, while peer reviewers praise the refined fMRI analysis without raising concerns about this limitation.

Perfect agreement on methodological innovation (C116, C119, C122). Both evaluations recognize the novelty of the pRF-based reconstruction approach. OpenEval notes limited comparison with inverted encoding models, while peer reviewers consistently praise the innovative paradigm and sophisticated analysis without raising this concern.

Strong agreement on location recovery findings (C9, C31, C44-47, C108). Both evaluations support the modeling approach and find the angular error results convincing. OpenEval provides detailed statistical interpretation, while peer reviewers praise the novel paradigm and ability to reliably recover attentional field parameters.

Strong agreement on width broadening effects (C10, C32, C51-53, C86, C109, C117, C126). Both evaluations affirm this as a key contribution supporting the zoom-lens model. OpenEval acknowledges the systematic overestimation issue, while peer reviewers accept the findings without raising concerns about this discrepancy.

Agreement on baseline findings (C58-60, C80-82). Both evaluations accept these null results. OpenEval interprets this as appropriate documentation that baseline activity was not systematically affected. Peer reviewers made a minor presentation suggestion about mentioning baseline offset but did not question the findings.

Disagreement on task difficulty dissociation (C128-131). OpenEval finds the behavioral data and non-monotonic accuracy changes support the dissociation claim. However, peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting concerns about whether differences are attributable solely to cue width changes and not confounded by task difficulty variations.

Strong agreement on summary conclusions (C149-152). Both evaluations affirm the significance of the findings. OpenEval finds the claims supported by collective evidence from behavioral, neural, and modeling results. Peer reviewers describe the study as valuable, addressing a gap in understanding attentional field representation and supporting the zoom-lens model.

Agreement on perceptual control experiment (C90, C94-96, C99-101, C103-105, C112-113, C120). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval notes the smaller sample size (n=5) and unexpected lack of V2 effect warrant caution. Peer reviewers accept the comprehensive analysis without raising these specific concerns.

Agreement on eye-tracking validation (C34-36, C188-191). Both evaluations support the fixation control as adequate. OpenEval emphasizes the methodological soundness of combining behavioral accuracy with eye-tracking validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the well-designed, methodologically rigorous study.

Agreement on behavioral validation (C29, C33, C106). Both evaluations support the behavioral data showing covert attention use. OpenEval provides detailed interpretation of statistical tests and above-chance performance. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the behavioral validation without raising concerns.

Agreement on temporal resolution analysis (C61-69, C83-85, C123). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive statistical tests and potential for dynamic tracking. Peer reviewers praise the sophisticated and methodologically rigorous analysis, implicitly accepting the temporal characterizations.

Agreement on gain modulation findings (C56, C121). Both evaluations support the V3 gain decrease with width and replication of prior work. OpenEval provides detailed statistical interpretation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the broader sophisticated analysis supporting attention models.

Partial overlap on gain findings (C54-55). Both evaluations support these statistical results. OpenEval discusses hierarchical gain differences and replication of prior work. Peer reviewers accept the null effects as part of the comprehensive, robust analysis.

Agreement on width overestimation (C87, C89, C111). Both evaluations accept these findings. OpenEval explicitly notes the systematic overestimation is acknowledged and investigated through perceptual control. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this aspect without raising concerns about the discrepancy.

Partial overlap on model performance (C48-49). Both evaluations support these findings about lack of systematic bias with cue width in V1/V2. OpenEval provides detailed statistical interpretation. Peer reviewers accept these as part of the novel and sophisticated modeling approach.

Partial overlap on temporal interval analysis (C70-72). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval discusses systematic temporal manipulation providing strong evidence for method's temporal resolution. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these detailed characterizations as supporting the method's utility.

OpenEval evaluated literature context and background claims (C1-5, C11-28, C114-115, C118, C124-125), finding them well-supported by appropriate citations and accurately characterizing the literature gap. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval evaluated future research suggestions (C132, C137-140, C142-143, C147-148, C153-154), finding them appropriate and well-reasoned proposals that logically extend from current findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these speculative future directions.
